content:Speaker user says: Can you provide a summary of how HARK works and what it is used for in educational settings? Answer according to: Home / Uncategorized / HARK, who goes there?
but the technology itself is something cool that could play a significant role in a not-too-distant future of education.
Yesterday I was able to join two faculty from UNC’s Physics department, two representatives from the Nomura Research Institute, and a final representative from Honda to learn about HARK. HARK grew out of Honda’s robotics lab as a hardware designed to allow robots to process complex and multi-source audio within a positional framework. That’s a bit much to process at once, so here’s a video demonstration.
The hardware is a dome-shaped object containing eight microphones that sits on a flat surface (preferably a flat surface perpendicular to the vector of gravity… of course), USB connectors, and on the device that I saw a printed band of alphabetically ordered letters surrounding the base.
The key features of the device are the ability to simultaneously record multiple sound inputs, differentiate and separate each of the inputs (over 90% reliability with 9 or fewer speakers) based on a fixed location, and work in the context of ambient or background noise.
At Honda they have used the HARK device alongside of analytical software to evaluate group participation and communication patterns within teams and students in corporate settings. HARK is able to measure total participation time, sequential conversation patterns, and interruptions. As an example one concept they operationalize is “influence”, which is defined as a pattern of interactions occurring after one person has spoken.
Analysis of the results according to HARK’s algorithm identifies three types of group participants: dominators, facilitators, and idea creators. These identities are conferred based on a few criteria including numbers of interruptions, total time talked, number of times talked (which could provide an average talking length), and patterns of interactions after a speaker has spoken. One interesting graphic is that interruptions are measured as a set of person to person interactions on a grid. Analysis of that grid can help to identify whether an individual equally interrupts everyone in the group, or only a single person.
The hope is that these analyses can operate with minimum work required by the faculty member, and operate at a scale to make it a benefit in a large class with multiple groups where a faculty or TA cannot always be present to actively view all interactions.
Within an educational setting there is a concept of an ideal grouping of three people: a manager, a skeptic, and a note-taker. You can see this outlined in a discussion for doing group work in a different physics class at http://groups.physics.umn.edu/physed/Research/CGPS/FAQcps.html. Conceptually this is an ideal arrangement of people for any type of group work, and is designed to produce optimal results. While we were unable to draw clear parallels between this taxonomy and what HARK produces (dominator, facilitator, idea generator), the form seems similar, and it was suggested that knowing these traits about members in a group could help to intentionally create groups that perform optimally.
A few items were noted as potential drawbacks with HARK.
When looking at how “influence” is operationalized it could be argued that this is not the best measure of influence, and it was additionally noted that all influence isn’t positive influence.
We brought up that the system is limited to only sound interpretation. Just because one person is not speaking does not mean that they are not engaged, as body language could indicate if that student was quiet, but also leaning forward into the conversation and actively listening.
There were questions regarding the construct validity of the three types of individuals identified, and whether this is a substantial enough taxonomy to effectively build groups. It would also be helpful to see data on the construct reliability of the HARK system – that is, whether it identifies students as accurately as a means tested group of faculty would.
Finally, at this point there seems to be a lot of work (some of it one-time) to plan for and make use of the HARK analysis. These preparatory steps include orienting the HARK device at each table (preferably in a manner that could not be tampered with), labeling and arranging seats around a table and keeping them relatively fixed, ensuring that students don’t relocate during a session, and then effecting data driven changes based on the analysis.
Ultimately, the faculty present felt that the HARK system did not confer enough of an ROI to make the cost of implementation worthwhile. They felt that they were not in a situation where the scale afforded would be necessary (they felt that they could already effectively observe the entire class), and that there was not yet enough data suggesting what optimal group assignment would be after class members were categorized. I and the faculty thought that there were opportunities for additional research both to establish those “what next?” best practices, as well as methods to make incorporation of the hardware easier in a large class setting.
One structural advantage is that because a single device can effectively differentiate between nine students, then it would not be necessary to have a number of HARK devices equal to the number of groups based on the arrangement of those groups in a class.
My own contribution is that this is a technology worth revisiting as natural language processing improves to be able to actively monitor each audio thread. Adequate growth in NLP/AI (Natural Language Processing/Artificail INtelarchitectures could help the system to be additionally effective in analyzing not only the interactions, but also the value of the content; it would know whether actively speaking members are actually speaking on topic, and additionally be able to isolate and surface for the faculty member themes across various groups.
I encourage you to check out the HARK page to see the other types of projects they’re working on. The one that catches my eye right away is the HARK-Kinect (the Microsoft visual input device for the Xbox) item. context:The speaker is seeking specific information regarding the financial expenses associated with implementing the HARK system within an educational environment. Baroque period (1600-1750)
Let’s start with the Baroque period, which is the earliest period of classical music. The Baroque period is famous for its ornate and elaborate style that is characterized by a complex texture and intricate melodies. The harpsichord is an iconic instrument of this period, and Johann Sebastian Bach is perhaps the most famous composer of the Baroque era.

Classical period (1750-1820)
The Classical period followed the Baroque period and is characterized by a simpler, cleaner, and more elegant style. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart is perhaps the most famous composer of the Classical period, and his music is some of the most loved and recognized in the world.

Mozart was a child prodigy, and he began composing at a very young age. His music is known for its delicate beauty, its elegance, and its emotional depth. We’ll hear a clip from his Symphony No. 40 in G minor.

Ludwig van Beethoven is perhaps the most famous composer of the Romantic period, and his music is considered to be some of the most important in the history of classical music. Beethoven’s music is known for its intense emotion and its dramatic power. We’ll hear a clip from his Symphony No. 5.

content:Speaker assistant says: Mozart and Beethoven were two of the greatest classical composers of all time. While they shared some similarities in their compositional style, they also had significant differences. Here are some key points to compare and contrast their styles:

Melodies:
Mozart's melodies tend to be elegant and graceful, with a focus on symmetrical phrases and balanced structure. His musical phrases are often similar in length and tend to move in a predictable, harmonious way. Beethoven's melodies are more dynamic and intense, with greater variation in length, contour, and harmonic progression. Beethoven often employs radical contrasts, unexpected pauses and abrupt shifts of tonality.

Harmony:
Both Mozart and Beethoven used classical forms such as sonatas, symphonies, and concertos, but Beethoven's harmonies are more adventurous and complex than Mozart's. Mozart emphasizes harmony primarily in creating an attractive musical landscape, whereas Beethoven uses harmony to create a sense of drama, conflict, and tension.

Rhythm:
Mozart's music often has a relatively straightforward, consistent rhythmic pulse that emphasizes melody and harmony. Beethoven's rhythm is more complex and irregular, ranging from rapid-fire runs of notes to sudden pauses that create a sense of tension.

Orchestration:
Mozart's orchestration is more traditionally classical, with a focus on balanced, delicate textures and clarity of individual lines. Beethoven's orchestration is more robust, with a wider range of instrumental colors, and he uses frequent contrasts between large and small ensembles to create dramatic effects.

Formal structure:
Both Mozart and Beethoven used classical forms such as the sonata-allegro, but Beethoven's compositions are often seen as pushing the boundaries of traditional forms. Beethoven's compositions frequently include experiments with new structures, innovative use of harmony, sudden changes of mood, and unconventional tonal relationships. Mozart, whilst enhancing and developing the classical form, remained within its framework.

In summary, while Mozart's style emphasizes elegance, grace, symmetry, and harmonic balance, Beethoven's style is more dynamic, complex, and innovative. Beethoven was known for his revolutionary style of composition and his tendency to take more risks in his work. Mozart, on the other hand, is celebrated for his impeccable craftsmanship and the sheer beauty of his melodies. context:This text compares and contrasts the distinct musical characteristics of Mozart and Beethoven, specifically analyzing differences in melody, harmony, rhythm, orchestration, and formal structure while highlighting their shared use of classical forms. keywords: Mozart, Beethoven, compositional style, classical forms, dynamic contrast tags: composers_style_analysis, mozart_beethoven_contrast, musical_technique_comparison, melodic_analysis, harmonic_complexity, rhythmic_variation, orchestration_styles, formal_structure_evolution

content:Speaker assistant says: Step 1: Choose the right beans
The quality of your coffee will depend largely on the beans you choose. High-quality beans will ensure you have a great cup of coffee. Look for freshly roasted, whole beans from reputable sources. Decide what flavor you prefer, and choose the roast that corresponds to it.

Step 2: Choose the correct brewing method
There are many brewing methods, and each has its own unique characteristics. Consider the equipment you have on hand, and choose the brewing method that best suits your needs. Some popular brewing methods include drip coffee, French press, espresso, and pour-over.

Step 3: Grind the beans to the right consistency
The type of brewing method you choose will determine how finely you should grind your beans. If you are using a drip coffee machine or a pour-over, look for a medium grind. For a French press, choose a coarse grind. And for espresso, you will need a fine grind.

Step 4: Ensure correct brewing time and temperature
The ideal water temperature for brewing coffee is around 195°F – 205°F. If the water is too hot, it will over-extract the coffee, making it bitter. If the water is too cold, it will under-extract the beans, producing a weak and flavorless cup. The brewing time will also vary depending on the brewing method used.

Step 5: Add flavor enhancements
If you want to enhance your coffee's flavor, there are a number of things you can do. Experiment with different creamers, sweeteners, or spices, like cinnamon or nutmeg. Consider using filtered water for a cleaner taste. A pinch of salt can balance out the coffee's bitterness.

Step 6: Enjoy
Pour yourself a cup of coffee, inhale the aroma, and savor the taste. Enjoy it black, or add cream or sweeteners as you see fit.

Conclusion:
Making a great cup of coffee doesn't have to be rocket science. With the right beans, the right brewing method, and the correct brewing time and temperature, you can easily produce a cup of coffee that will rival the best coffee shops out there. content:Speaker assistant says: Coffee Pastry Cream-Filled Croissants

Ingredients:
- 1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
- 1/4 tsp salt
- 1/4 tsp instant yeast
- 1/2 cup cold unsalted butter, cut into small pieces
- 1/2 cup cold water
- 1 tbsp instant espresso powder
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar
- 2 egg yolks
- 1 cup milk
- 1/4 cup cornstarch
- 1 tsp vanilla extract
- 1/4 cup heavy cream
- Powdered sugar, for dusting

Instructions:

1. In a large mixing bowl, combine the flour, salt, and instant yeast. Add the cold butter and use your hands or a pastry blender to work it into the flour mixture until crumbly.

2. In a small bowl, whisk together the cold water and instant espresso powder until dissolved. Add this to the flour mixture and stir until the dough comes together. Cover the dough and refrigerate overnight.

3. The next day, preheat the oven to 400°F. On a floured surface, roll out the dough into a rectangle shape about 1/4 inch thick. Fold the dough into thirds like a letter, then roll it out again and fold it up again. Repeat this process 4-5 times.

4. Cut the dough into triangles and roll them up tightly, starting at the widest end and rolling towards the tip. Place the croissants on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper and let them rise in a warm place for 30 minutes.

5. Bake the croissants for 15-20 minutes, or until golden brown. Let them cool to room temperature.

6. While the croissants are cooling, make the coffee pastry cream filling. In a medium saucepan, whisk together the granulated sugar and egg yolks until thick and pale. Stir in the milk and cornstarch, then cook over medium heat until the mixture thickens.

7. Remove the pan from the heat and stir in the vanilla extract and heavy cream. Let the pastry cream cool to room temperature.

8. Once the croissants are cooled, use a sharp knife to carefully slice them in half horizontally. Spoon the coffee pastry cream into the croissants and top with the other half of the croissant. Dust with powdered sugar before serving. Enjoy your coffee-filled pastry and happy Mother's Day! context:The recipe provides a guide for Coffee Pastry Cream-Filled Croissants, incorporating espresso powder into both the dough and the filling, ideal for a Mother's Day treat. keywords: croissants, pastry cream, coffee ingredients tags: dessert_requests, coffee_dessert_integration, recipe_suggestions, dessert_collection, croissants, pastry_cream, espresso_powder

content:Speaker assistant says: Absolutely! Here's the recipe for Irish Cream and Coffee Cookies with the Irish Cream Italian meringue buttercream frosting:

For the cookies:

Ingredients:
- 1/2 cup unsalted butter, at room temperature
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar
- 1/2 cup brown sugar
- 1 egg
- 1 tsp vanilla extract
- 1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
- 1/2 tsp baking soda
- 1/2 tsp baking powder
- 1 tsp salt
- 1/4 cup instant coffee granules
- 1/4 cup Irish cream liqueur

Directions:

1. Preheat the oven to 375°F. Line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

2. In a large mixing bowl, cream together the butter, granulated sugar, and brown sugar until light and fluffy.

3. Beat in the egg and vanilla extract until well combined.

4. In a separate mixing bowl, whisk together the flour, baking soda, baking powder, and salt.

5. Add the dry ingredients to the wet ingredients and mix until just combined.

6. In a small bowl or cup, stir together the instant coffee granules and Irish cream liqueur until the coffee granules are dissolved.

7. Add the coffee mixture to the cookie dough and stir until well combined.

8. Drop heaping tablespoons of dough onto the prepared baking sheet, leaving about 2 inches between each cookie.

9. Bake for 12-15 minutes, or until the cookies are set and lightly browned around the edges.

10. Let the cookies cool on the baking sheet for 5 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack to cool completely.

For the frosting:

Ingredients:
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar
- 1/4 cup water
- 2 egg whites
- 1/2 cup unsalted butter, at room temperature
- 1/4 cup Irish cream liqueur

Directions:

1. In a small saucepan, combine the granulated sugar and water. Heat over medium-high heat, stirring until the sugar is dissolved.

2. Increase the heat to high and bring the mixture to a boil. Insert a candy thermometer into the mixture and cook until the temperature reaches 240°F.

3. In a large mixing bowl, beat the egg whites with an electric mixer until they form soft peaks.

4. Slowly pour the hot sugar syrup into the egg whites while continuing to beat with the mixer.

5. Beat the frosting on high speed until it cools to room temperature and forms stiff peaks.

6. Beat in the butter and Irish cream liqueur until smooth and creamy.

To assemble:

1. Spread a generous dollop of frosting onto the flat side of one cookie.

2. Top with another cookie, flat side down, to make a sandwich.

3. Repeat with remaining cookies and frosting.

4. Serve chilled or at room temperature. content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Here is the recipe for Andrea's Hand Cranked Coffee Cavatelli:

Ingredients:
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 1/4 cup instant coffee powder
- 2 eggs
- 1/2 cup water
- 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
- 1/2 tsp salt
- 1/4 tsp black pepper
- 1 lb mixed wild mushrooms, trimmed and sliced
- 2 garlic cloves, minced
- 1/4 cup freshly grated Parmesan cheese
- 1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley

Instructions:

1. In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the flour and instant coffee powder.

2. In a small mixing bowl, whisk together the eggs, water, extra-virgin olive oil, salt, and black pepper.

3. Add the egg mixture to the flour mixture and stir until a dough forms.

4. Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for a few minutes, until smooth and elastic.

5. Divide the dough into 4 equal parts and roll each part into a long, thin rope, about 1/2 inch in diameter.

6. Use a sharp knife to cut the ropes into small pieces, about 1/2 inch in length.

7. Using a cavatelli maker or gnocchi board, roll the pieces of dough into cavatelli shapes, pressing each piece down lightly with your thumb and dragging it towards you to form a small tube shape.

8. Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add the cavatelli and cook for 2-3 minutes, or until they float to the surface. Reserve 1/4 cup of the pasta cooking water.

9. While the pasta is cooking, heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the sliced mushrooms and cook for 5-7 minutes, or until golden brown and tender.

10. Add the minced garlic to the skillet and cook for another minute, until fragrant.

11. Drain the cavatelli and add them to the skillet with the mushrooms and garlic. Toss to combine.

12. Add the reserved pasta cooking water, grated Parmesan cheese, and chopped fresh parsley to the skillet. Toss to combine.

13. Serve the cavatelli hot, topped with additional Parmesan cheese and chopped parsley, if desired.
